new_statements.quote: 2 - 4 Le mot a une fonction dans la phrase. Il est composé de syllabes et correspond au mot grammatical. I - L'accent d'intensité tombe sur la première syllabe sauf dans les disyllabiques qui se terminent sur / a /. Ceux-ci ont 1'accent [sic, = l'accent] d'intensité sur la deuxième syllabe. II - On trouve les phonèmes m, n, ŋ, 1, d, p, k, à la fin du mot, mais seul l'allophone de / k /, [ x ] se présente exclusivement dans cette position. / p / et / k / marquent la limite des mots.
new_statements.translation: 2-4 The word has a function in the sentence. It is composed of syllables and corresponds to the grammatical word. I - The stress (accent of intensity) falls on the first syllable, except in disyllables that end in /a/; these have the stress on the second syllable. II - The phonemes m, n, ŋ, l, d, p, k occur word-finally, but only the allophone [x] of /k/ occurs exclusively in this position. /p/ and /k/ mark word boundaries.
new_statements.citation: Perrin, Mona J. & Margaret V. Hill. 1969. Mambila (parler d'Atta): description phonologique. Yaoundé: Université Fédérale du Cameroun, Section de Linguistique Appliquée [SIL Cameroon re-edition with IPA symbols, 2008; SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 1728].
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 'Remarques liminaires', §2-4 'Le mot', point I; p. 7 of the 2008 re-edition (PDF page 8)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (71 pp., text layer; the PDF's metadata Subject 'Mambila Phonology, Atta Reference Dialect, revised slightly 2008', Author 'Perrin & Hill'). extracted text of PDF page 8 (printed p. 7), ch. 2 'Remarques liminaires', sec. 2-4 'Le mot', point I reads exactly: 'L'accent d'intensité tombe sur la première syllabe sauf dans les disyllabiques qui se terminent sur / a /. Ceux-ci ont 1'accent d'intensité sur la deuxième syllabe.' followed by point II on word-final phonemes and '/ p / et / k / marquent la limite des mots.' The reported quote matches character for character (the '[sic, = l'accent]' is the first reader's gloss on the digit-1-for-l typo that is in the PDF). READING: I read…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level intensity stress is on the first syllable of the (phonological = grammatical) word; the only stated exception is disyllabic words ending in /a/, which are stressed on the second (final) syllable. Stress is described independently of the four-level lexical/grammatical tone system (every syllable bears at least one tone). Most words are mono- or disyllabic; trisyllables are compounds, loans, or N̩-initial.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables ending in /a/ take stress on the second syllable (note that the authors treat VV sequences such as [nea⁴] 'four', [gua²a¹] 'swim' as vowel sequences, so CVa/CVVa items may fall under this clause as well as CVCa words).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is 'le mot' in a tagmemic phonological hierarchy (discourse > paragraph > phrase > word > syllable), explicitly equated with the grammatical word; based on elicited words, sentences and texts from three Atta speakers (1968-69) at 'débit moyen'. Language has 4 level tones; stress statement is a brief remark, not instrumentally supported.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the Atta lect ('parler d'Atta', Tikar Plain, Adamaoua, Cameroon; data collected at Atta 1968-69 after 4 weeks at Gembu, Nigeria, 1967). Connell (Four tones and downtrend, mambila.info) states that his Somié variety is 'referred to locally as Ba' and 'differs little from the Atta/Sonkolong varieties (also Ba) discussed by Perrin'. In Glottolog 5.3's dialect tree, Ba [juba1238] sits under Western Mambila [nige1255, ISO mzk], whereas came1252 'Donga Mambila' comprises Kabri, Kara, Maberem, Ngubin and Titong (Connell's 'Bundu' / East Mambila cluster on the Nigerian plateau). Glottolog nevertheless files Hill & Perrin 1969 under came1252 (language code 'Atta = Ba Mambila = Cameroon Mambila [mcu]'), following the ISO split mcu = Cameroon Mambila. So: first-hand statement for Atta/Ba Mambila; its assignment to came1252 rests on the ISO [mcu] convention, and under Glottolog 5.3's internal classification it would rather belong to nige1255 (dialect juba1238). No phonological description of the Donga/East Mambila lects proper (Kabri, Kara, Titong, Maberem, Ngubin) was found beyond Connell's comparative survey wordlists.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the source of the catalog's existing statement ('fixed: initial syllable'); the passage is present verbatim at the stated locator (p. 7 = PDF p. 8) and the reading is confirmed. The existing statement's quote is truncated before the tonal remark of §2-5; the work should be recorded as a four-tone language with an initial-stress statement plus the /a/-final disyllable exception.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (accent d'intensité) is on the first syllable of the word; the one stated exception class is disyllabic words ending in /a/, which are stressed on the second (final) syllable. The language is at the same time tonal: four level tones numbered 1-4 plus five contour tones, every syllable carrying at least one tone (§2-5, §5-1). No interaction between stress and tone is discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables ending in /a/ take the stress on the second syllable (§2-4 I). Nothing else.
new_statements.identity_note: Perrin & Hill 1969 is based on data gathered at Atta, Cameroon (11 Jan 1968 - 20 Jan 1969) from three Atta-born informants, after four weeks at Gembu, Nigeria in 1967 (§1-2, p. 5); it is the Atta variety the Glottolog entry names. Ndiola Tsuata 2004 describes the same Cameroon 'jù bá' dialect (Atta, Somié, Songkolong). Connell 2007 describes Len, a Western Mambila lect adjacent to the Grassfields, a different variety.
